[Thus begins the description of the virtues of a friend:
O friend, friend, prosperity, intelligence, and auspiciousness are bestowed by a friend; a loyal servant accomplishes firm tasks and achieves victory in battle with confidence.
A bond of friendship is not severed again and again; yet if a friend becomes an enemy, even a kinsman of one's own clan is tormented.

A servant is a friend for every task; a servant is a servant at every command. When a servant is absent, wealth perishes; a servant is the fruit of the enemy's wailing. (PrāPi. 37 [Chappaa]) If a seated friend shows even a slight sign of some business, [it is accomplished].

[The Paṅkāvalī metre:

If the first foot consists of six *gaṇas* and the second foot has its thorns shaken off (consists of four *laghus*), and one knows that there are sixteen *kalās* in each foot, Piṅgala declares that it is the *Paṅkāvalī*. (PrāPi. 148)
Just as one who is born of noble lineage is possessed of virtue, so too is he who performs a favor for another with a smile.

In the first foot, there is a *kaṇṇa* (four *ga*s) and a *païjja* (one *ga* and two *la*s); in the second, a *jagaṇa* (two *la*s and one *ga*) at the end; and in that foot, there are four horses (*turaṅga*—four *la*s) and a *saaṇa* (one *ga* and two *la*s). This is the *Vasantatilakā* meter with fourteen syllables.
Furthermore, the *Vasantatilakā* meter, composed by the serpent [Kālidāsa], is recited with relish by the best of poets who have seen it; it is flavorful and delightful.
